title: S House / BOV ESTUDIO / BOV ESTUDIO
text:
S House / BOV ESTUDIO / BOV ESTUDIO

In Ayllón (Segovia), adjacent to the historic center, the openings of a 1910 facade now look out onto a courtyard. The facade originally belonged to a family home that was divided into two dwellings in the mid-1940s. Decades later, the owner reunited one of those halves with two adjacent plots to build his primary residence. He wanted a house that could be navigated without steps, and where proximity to the street was compatible with family privacy.

title: Fig Tree House / Estúdio Lava
text:
Fig Tree House / Estúdio Lava

The construction of a residence at Praia da Figueira in Angra dos Reis faced the challenge of being built on a sloped terrain with dense Atlantic Forest vegetation. The semicircular shape stems from the intention to orient the building towards both the sunset and the open sea horizon across the island of Gipóia.

title: Espira Yoga Shala / Arquitectura Mixta
text:
Espira Yoga Shala / Arquitectura Mixta

Inspired by the delicate wings of Costa Rica's glasswing butterfly, Espira explores the relationship between lightness, balance, and suspended movement through a sculptural bamboo structure. Located within the Peninsula Papagayo Sports Complex in Guanacaste, Costa Rica, the Yoga Shala translates these natural qualities into an open architectural form designed to encourage stillness, awareness, and a deeper connection with the surrounding landscape.

title: Intermodal Hub of Lousada / spaceworkers
text:
Intermodal Hub of Lousada / spaceworkers

The planned intervention is located in the northern area of Lousada, a growing zone where new residential clusters, cultural spaces, and an expanded road network are being proposed to integrate with existing infrastructure. The intervention site has a strong cultural dynamic, supported by the Music Conservatory and, more recently, the opening of the Romanesque Interpretation Center. This new cultural hub has contributed to the revitalization of the area and to Lousada's northern expansion, reinforcing its identity as a key cultural district.

title: Verrière House / Projectoire
text:
Verrière House / Projectoire

The project involves the extension of an old barn that had previously been converted into a family residence. Located in Potton, a township bordered to the south by the Canada–United States border and the state of Vermont, the site is bucolic, surrounded by the mountains of the Eastern Townships.

title: Villa Dellago / JM Architecture
text:
Villa Dellago / JM Architecture

Villa Dellago is a private villa located in the natural landscape of the east shore of Garda Lake, in Italy.

title: Argentine Media Library / CONTINUO ARCHITECTURE
text:
Argentine Media Library / CONTINUO ARCHITECTURE

Located in the Argentine neighbourhood of Beauvais, France, the new Argentine Media Library is part of a major urban regeneration programme. Designed by CONTINUO ARCHITECTURE, the project aims to create a new cultural landmark, strengthening the relationship between architecture, public space and community life.

title: Engineered Waterways: What Architecture Can Learn from Urban Canals
text:
Engineered Waterways: What Architecture Can Learn from Urban Canals

Unlike open coastlines or the edges of natural bodies of water, urban canals are narrow, linear, engineered landscapes that cut decisively through the urban fabric. Where rivers follow the contours of a landscape and shape the landform, canals impose their geometry and logic, redefining the relationship between architecture and water. Their edges are clearly defined, often shaped by retaining walls, embankments, and the infrastructure that supports movement along and across the water. Bridges, pedestrian walkways, mooring points, and docks establish a distinctive relationship between the waterway and its context, creating an urban environment where the boundaries between water and architecture are realized.

title: Housing on the Marshes / OFIS Architects
text:
Housing on the Marshes / OFIS Architects

Housing on the Marshes is located along Ljubljana's Path of Remembrance, where the urban fabric meets the landscape of the Ljubljana Marshes. The neighbourhood comprises 170 apartments and two commercial spaces. Its design connects collective housing with planted terraces, shared outdoor areas and a landscape shaped by water, soft ground and a long history of settlement.

title: What Lies Behind the Walls of Contemporary Bathrooms
text:
What Lies Behind the Walls of Contemporary Bathrooms

In 1966, architect and researcher Alexander Kira published "The Bathroom: Criteria for Design", a study that challenged conventional approaches to bathroom planning. Drawing on research into human anatomy, physiology, ergonomics, and personal hygiene practices, Kira questioned whether standardized bathroom fixtures adequately responded to the needs of their users. His work proposed reconsidering these environments through the relationship between the human body and its surroundings, rather than relying exclusively on established dimensions and arrangements.

title: Latin America in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Civic Life, and Heritage Conservation
text:
Latin America in Focus: This Month in Architecture, Civic Life, and Heritage Conservation

This edition of Latin America in Focus explores the ways architecture shapes collective life across different scales and contexts, from public infrastructure and educational environments to the urban histories that continue to inform cities today. The featured projects in Ecuador and Mexico consider how cultural facilities and landscape interventions can support shared activities while responding to their surroundings, while the history of Santo Domingo traces the early development of colonial urban planning in the Americas. The selection also looks at current approaches to cultural heritage conservation and public space, highlighting initiatives in Peru and across the region.

title: The Ribbon / Orms
text:
The Ribbon / Orms

The Ribbon is a new mixed-use development designed by Orms for M&G Real Estate and CBRE Development Management, occupying a prominent corner site at the junction of Oxford Street and Wells Street in central London. The 100,000 sq ft building provides office accommodation above retail space and a basement venue, completing a key gateway site between Oxford Street and Fitzrovia.

title: ZHA’s Recently Completed Théâtre Royal de Rabat in Morocco Photographed by Hufton+Crow
text:
ZHA’s Recently Completed Théâtre Royal de Rabat in Morocco Photographed by Hufton+Crow

The Théâtre Royal de Rabat performing arts complex is located on the left bank of the Bou Regreg River in Rabat, Morocco. Conceived by Zaha Hadid Architects (ZHA) in 2010, it was partially inaugurated in October 2024 and opened to the public on April 22, 2026. The project is part of a cultural development initiative led by King Mohammed VI and stands near the Mausoleum of Mohammed V and the Hassan Tower, a historic minaret. The Royal Theatre of Rabat Foundation oversees the institution's management and its cultural program, which includes concerts, dance, symphony, and theater. A few months after the opening, ZHA has released photography by Hufton+Crow that shows the building's architecture.

title: Caring for Life Across Scales: The XIV Ibero-American Biennial in Brasília
text:
Caring for Life Across Scales: The XIV Ibero-American Biennial in Brasília

Caring for life: this was the motto of the XIV edition of the Ibero-American Architecture Biennial (BIAU) held in Brasília from November 3 to 6, 2026. The choice of care as a theme is significant, as is its presentation as an infinitive verb—lacking tense or mood—serving as an urgent call to action. Structured around the thematic axes of water, vegetation, housing, communities, and new territories, the discussions made it clear that these elements are not mere resources or means for caring for life. Rather, they must be understood as subjects of care, demanding an attentive and respectful consideration of their natural and social cycles within architectural practice.

title: SHISHI Dates Cafe / Naqsh architectural & engineering consultancy
text:
SHISHI Dates Cafe / Naqsh architectural & engineering consultancy

Located within the industrial fabric of Al Quoz, Dubai, SHI SHI brings together the worlds of production, retail, hospitality, and work within a single architectural environment. Designed by NAQSH Architecture, the project explores how the utilitarian character of a factory can coexist with the warmth and intimacy of a café and boutique. Rather than concealing the rawness associated with its industrial setting, the design embraces it as the foundation of its architectural identity.

title: Title Roll Building / Cho and Partners
text:
Title Roll Building / Cho and Partners

The back streets of Sinsa-dong – Sinsa-dong has a strongly commercial character. It was once a quiet area of houses and low-rise multi-unit buildings rather than apartment complexes, with small cafes and shops, but commercial development has gradually taken over. The project sits on a back street between Sinsa and Apgujeong stations, connected to Dosan-daero and very close to the main road.

title: Peacock Forest Retreat / line+ studio
text:
Peacock Forest Retreat / line+ studio

Nestled in a forested valley in northeastern China, Peacock Forest Retreat is a hospitality project that integrates mountain resort experiences with Buddhist rituals and meditation. Designed by line+ studio and completed in March 2023, the project brings together guest accommodation, dining, social spaces, spa and fitness facilities, and contemplative spaces within a continuous architectural and landscape sequence.

title: High Andean Refuge in Quichuay / Pircanato / Pircanato
text:
High Andean Refuge in Quichuay / Pircanato / Pircanato

The High Andean Refuge in Quichuay integrates contemporary materials and production methods with traditional techniques from the Peruvian highlands through an experimental construction system. It is designed to respond to the extreme climatic conditions of the high Andean territory and provide architectural solutions with replicable habitability criteria for rural communities.

title: Modular Bahia / UNA Barbara e Valentim
text:
Modular Bahia / UNA Barbara e Valentim

Between the river and the sea, on the southern coast of Bahia, the Modular Bahia project proposes a contemporary tropical retreat, sensitive to the local territory and climate. Developed by UNA barbara e valentim, the project combines industrialized solutions with bioclimatic strategies - responding precisely to environmental conditions and the desire for a more landscape-integrated occupation.

title: Casa Lucerna / Belen Ilarri Studio
text:
Casa Lucerna / Belen Ilarri Studio

A modest 1970s house had a hidden spatial quality beneath a suspended ceiling.  The intervention begins with this discovery, reorganising the house and recovering a height that completely transforms the perception of space. How can a home be transformed without erasing what makes it unique?

title: The Carmine House / NPS Arquitectos
text:
The Carmine House / NPS Arquitectos

The property consists of a series of platforms that overcome the difference in height between the streets adjacent to the land (approximately 12 metres). On the upper level, there were already some buildings, which appeared somewhat fragmented. The proposal sought to unite these fragments, outlining a U-shape that defines a patio to the east and recovers the old threshing floor to the south/west. The ends of the new shape start at the pre-existing buildings and join to the west with a new body that, while maintaining its shape, stands out for its tectonics.

title: Zunli Tea House / OUT OF OFFICE DESIGN
text:
Zunli Tea House / OUT OF OFFICE DESIGN

Zunli Tea House occupies an old dwelling in Suzhou's historic Gusu district. The owner wanted to bring the intimacy and changing views of a classical Chinese garden into everyday domestic life. A modest budget, restrictions attached to the property's tenancy and the building's fragile condition set clear limits on the renovation. The original room arrangement had to be retained, opportunities for reinforcement were limited, and walls could not be cut into or chased for services. Electrical conduits were therefore surface-mounted, while furniture, planting and finishes became the principal means of reshaping the interior.

title: Fulldraw Winery / Clayton Korte
text:
Fulldraw Winery / Clayton Korte

Fulldraw Vineyard is located within the Templeton Gap AVA, the heart of California's Central Coast wine country. Set on 100 acres of established vineyards, the land is characterized by its rich limestone soils and cool maritime climate—the perfect setting for growing Rhone-style varietals. Tucked into the rolling terrain, the winery is accessed via a long, looping drive taking visitors through the vineyards before arriving at their destination. The proprietors, Connor and Rebecca McMahon tasked Clayton Korte with designing a winery that represents their personality and passion for winemaking. The solution is a winery that is familiar yet exclusive, comfortable yet sophisticated—seemingly disparate ideas that come together through a visitor experience that is as curated as it is intimate.

title: Central Kitchen Graz / Superfuturegroup
text:
Central Kitchen Graz / Superfuturegroup

The new Central Kitchen Graz combines the requirements of a large-scale food production facility with an architectural concept focused on sustainability, circular economy principles, and high-quality working environments. Approximately 15,000 meals are prepared and distributed to municipal childcare facilities and social welfare institutions every day.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

AI has sped up how teams design and build, but quality assurance (QA) testing hasn’t kept pace, and the web may be getting less accessible. Drawing on new research, Andrew Chung explains what separates the teams whose accessibility efforts are keeping up, and how to embed human judgment into AI-enabled workflows without slowing delivery.

title: Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams
text:
Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

An AI feature can save users time on a task, only for them to spend it checking the results. This practical audit helps product teams decide where AI earns its place and what users need to verify its output.

title: A New Community For In-House UX People
text:
A New Community For In-House UX People

We’ve been working on something new! We’ve teamed up for a **new small community** for people doing UX-inside organizations — with weekly calls and a shared library of the business cases, templates, and research plans that have actually worked for other folks. [Jump to details](https://uxinsiders.boagworld.com/).

title: Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible
text:
Making Immersive LLM Chat Experiences More Accessible

As LLM chat patterns become more widespread, making them accessible is essential to ensuring everyone can access the information, tools, and opportunities they offer. Drawing on his work improving these interfaces, Eric Bailey shares practical ways to make chat-based experiences on the web more accessible and usable for people who rely on assistive technology.

title: Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex
text:
Modern CSS Might Make Your Front-End More Complex

Replacing JavaScript with a modern CSS feature can simplify a piece of code while making the wider application harder to reason about. Gabriel Shoyombo explores what happens when logic is split between CSS and JavaScript, sharing practical guidance to help you keep complexity in check during migration.

title: A Spark Of Color In November’s Gray (2026 Wallpapers Edition)

A Spark Of Color In November’s Gray (2026 Wallpapers Edition)

Let’s kick of November with a new collection of desktop wallpapers! Designed by creatives from across the globe, the wallpapers come in a variety of screen resolutions and can be downloaded for free. Enjoy!

title: Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?
text:
Accordion Icons: Which Work Best?

A closer look at accordion icons, why split menus are harmful, and why it’s better not to have icons and text labels link to different actions. Plus, why the caret is the safest icon choice. You’ll find more [useful guides](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/category/guides/) and [online workshops](https://smashingconf.com/online-workshops) here on Smashing Magazine, so make sure to browse and explore.

title: Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function
text:
Embracing Playful Imperfection With The CSS `random()` Function

Design systems thrive on consistency, so where does randomness fit in? Through playful demos of organic typography, bouncing letters, and splayed cards, Brecht De Ruyte shows how the new CSS `random()` function brings a little imperfection to the web without JavaScript libraries or preprocessor loops that generate hundreds of lines of static CSS.

text:
Is Your Organization Messing Up AI Adoption?

What can digital transformation teach us about AI adoption? Paul Boag revisits his book Digital Adaptation to show how lessons from the past can help organizations navigate the challenges of AI today.

title: How I use AI as a solo designer
text:
How I use AI as a solo designer

Things that work well, and things that kind of failed.

I’ve been part of a growing 30+ strong design team for 6 years — a great team with a wide skill set, within a large organization. When AI became popular, Figma Make was the natural thing to try, as it lived within Figma, with a few specks of usage in Gemini and assisted user interviews (Maze), resulting in tiny glimpses of impact. Things changed quite a lot in January, as I’ve decided to take on a new challenge in a B2B e-comm scale-up as a solo UXer.

Suddenly, I faced a wall of work: support features in flight, drive discovery work, improve processes, user research, prototype, set up guidelines…the amount of split focus was scary in the beginning. I did however, see that design had the opportunity to contribute with clarity; to drive a future experience that solves user problems in a more focused way. For that to happen, though, I needed to be able to focus myself. All of this combined with the intriguing launch of Claude Code to Figma, reignited my curiosity about AI.

Prototyping with Claude Code

This works well, dangerously well | Using it almost daily.

To say that anything killed Figma is kind of lazy and silly. It’s not that I care too much about Figma, it’s more about the creative freedom to move an element from A to B in any way I want, directly on a canvas, with no intermediary interaction. Why would I give up drawing digitally with superpowers, or force myself to learn any other tool for this? However, I do think tools like Figma provided underwhelming prototyping capabilities, for far too long. Specialised software came in e.g. Axure, Protopie and excelled within their niche, but led to multi-tool management, had their own constraints and still felt slow at times. This is where AI filled in a gap, for me, especially useful being on my own.

I’ve only built maybe one or two Figma click through prototypes since February. Prototyping with Claude Code enables me to express rich, complex interactions, much much faster. Practically, I often sketch ideas and tons of alternatives on paper, then materialise some of those layouts in Figma, fleshing out multiple states too. For longer, more complex journeys, I rely on FigJam diagrams too. Then I bring it all to life in Claude Code with prompts, focusing on interactions, motion and flows, resulting in a local working prototype, usually as a single .html file. It’s not always in this order, sometimes I skip steps, but it’s always a loop. The .html file is then published online, in a private prototype hub using Figma Make. The truth is always in the live web version. Technically, I can get from one end to another in only a few minutes…which allows me to iterate a lot, in many directions. The number of big or small loops until I get to a good design though… no idea, I always lose count. (Since I’ve started writing this Claude Code just released Artifacts, which I’ll test as a way to publish prototypes).

Overall, it’s been easier for me, devs, PMs, users, pretty much everyone involved in the process of building something, to interact and feel flows instead of imagining how static Figma frames move. Interpretation of how flows connect and behave often led to divergent implementation in the past, so this helped with consistency as well. What I miss in prototyping with AI is tracking relevant variety, as I explore and test. This can happen across an entire flow, on a page layout, or within a tiny component. I need something that enables me to save variation on any level, based on context and hypothesis. To deal with this, I often hide little settings panels to switch variations, but now I’m exploring a lab-like setup to visualise prototype variety on a flow and element level.

There’s a downside to speed, though. In the beginning, I had the tendency to either jump into AI too quickly, or prompt a few too many times focusing on unnecessary details within a single direction, just because I could. Rookie mistake; associating a polished interaction and flow with a good experience. That’s something I noticed happening among the team too, with devs, PMs, others using AI to prototype, but we’ve started keeping each other accountable by going back to goals, research, testing, stepping away from the tool. Overall, given the right control and focus, this is a part of AI that helps me tremendously to build a better product and gives me back extra time to either collect feedback earlier and iterate, or explore alternatives instead of spending it on tooling.

Usability testing

This works well | Using it a lot

A critical point of usability testing is to give people a scenario and a clear task to be completed, then step away and shut up; let them voice their thoughts and observe what they do. The more you interrupt with “sorry, this doesn’t work; it’s just a prototype…oh…that doesn’t work either”, the less likely you are to capture a full end-to-end experience. For me, turning concepts into fully working prototypes enabled exactly this: back up and observe. Being a B2B back-end ecommerce tool, UIs and flows can get quite complex, especially when tables are at the core. Having the possibility to express a lot of depth lets participants try different pathways to achieve their goal, which in turn enabled me and the team to learn more about their mental models. There are still dead ends and not all states are covered, but prototyping with AI has given me the chance to be intentional in this aspect too. Questions as “what did you expect to happen” are now focused on parts of the experience that I truly wish to learn about, not a consequence of tooling constraints.

Adjusting context for each session and carrying data across a flow become way easier too. We’re working with different kinds of companies selling all sorts of things, from electronics to fashion. Now, as late as 15 min before a session starts, I just tell Claude “change products in this prototype to be about electronics” and it’s done. This level of nuance and detail brings a natural feeling into the research session. When it comes to carrying data over, since flows are complex, it’s important to reflect real values, sometimes created by the user, e.g., setting a product’s price, selecting a certain number of products to publish, etc. When these values don’t match across the flow, it tends to distract some participants, once again interrupting their experience.

User research synthesis

This works well | Using it biweekly

I had the chance to study different ways of coding user research, mostly within academia; it was pure research done without chasing economic impact for a product; quite refreshing to do once in a while. In a nutshell, coding is analyzing your research by going back through documentation such as recordings, notes, diaries, etc., and highlighting findings to eventually extract common themes. Handling all this data requires a lot of mental effort, but leads to a deep connection and understanding of users, while reflecting on the quality of your own method. However, realistically, I can’t spend a week analyzing interviews or testing sessions, creating video clips, documenting, and presenting it all as well…as much as I love doing this detective kind of work.

Therefore, I’ve been experimenting with different degrees of AI usage when synthesizing data and I’ve noticed something. Let’s say I conduct a series of 8 user interviews and discover a bunch of problems with a feature across all sessions. Since everything is recorded in Google Meet, I then ask Gemini to merge all sessions and extract common themes, quotes, and action points. This is lightning fast. However, a couple of weeks in, I recall very few of these findings, having to constantly go back to double-check what they meant. On top of that, a lot of nuance is getting lost in AI’s own interpretation and writing style. It all becomes a bit too generic or even worse, insights get skewed with words and expressions participants never used(often even when guided not to do this). The less I handle the insights myself, the less they get embedded into my design mind. I feel less confident in early design decisions, diminishing my ability to advocate for them among stakeholders.

It would be foolish to just ignore the huge advantage of speed. Currently, I use Gemini to summarise individual interviews, but also write down timestamps during the session to know which parts to rewatch, turn into clips to be shared with the team, and extract genuine quotes. Having another person join to take notes and observe helps too. I then take all the summaries and run them through AI just like before, but don’t use the outcome directly. I treat AI as a super text editor, mostly useful to validate occurrences of words and expressions, within large amounts of input. Now, I rely on those key timeframes, myself and the note taker to really form common themes and capture nuance instead. Usually, a couple of weeks later, I also force myself to go through a couple of sessions to get reconnected to participants. For now this feels like a good balance of speed and quality. It gives me back time that I use to phrase and share insights, or to run more research.

New visual directions

This was meh.. | Tried a couple of times only

Part of improving the current experience is a refreshed interface. The product’s functionality has grown over the years, but the UI hasn’t always kept this pace, so it was time to present all that power and data more clearly. It’s an interesting exercise, trying to capture enough of the product scope to understand core user problems without being trapped in too many edge cases and constraints. My instinct said that we needed something clear, bear bones that lets the content shine, while leveraging a few playful elements used in external materials. Nevertheless, it’s the kind of activity that requires a lot of mental space; and something that I’ve never done without a design team around. Comparing perspectives born from a similar affinity of solving other people’s problems has always been a really fun part of the process for me. That’s how I hoped to use AI too; to fill in this gap, and to have a fellow (junior?) designer next to me.

I was also hoping there was a big enough pool of training data to make AI work well for these types of elements our product mostly consists of (data dashboards, graphs, complex tables, and product cards). I was mostly looking for diversity in visual expression both in interfaces and interactions in core steps of the product. I’ve never expected end-to-end flows and perfectly tweaked screens to just pick up. Practically, I’ve tried Figma Make, Claude Code in Figma, Claude Design, and Google Stitch and I’ve been feeding them different kinds of contexts, data and prompts to get diversity in outcome.

The interesting takes, mostly from Claude Design and Google Stitch were getting a bit far from the brief, but in a fun way, sparking a few thoughts. Some of these turned into ideas for functionality that might or might not lead to anything, or made me wonder about details as typography scales, spacing, and elevation. Many results simply validated directions I didn’t want to take, being impractical or way too expressive, which is valuable in a way. Sadly, nothing was solid enough to inspire me to chase an entirely new direction and AI didn’t come close to being a sparring partner; it lacked the depth I was looking for, and overall like it went literally out of the box without a real purpose; the kind of quick and dirty exploration you’d do in between meetings, or Friday afternoon, that you look back at later “hmm… what was I thinking…”

To be fair, I do think that if one spends more time to iterate on guiding the AI, perhaps feeding it a more precise combination of inputs and skills, you could probably get better results. I’m saying this as things are evolving fast, and also after seeing skills like this take one, an attempt at applying Nothing’s visual style to dashboard UIs.

UX feedback skill

This works well | In trial for adoption

User research in the B2B space is quite different from research for B2C products, where I used to have quick access to a large panel of users within tools, agencies, or by simply walking outside... Even with the help of customer facing teams, reaching specific users takes time and effort — making it challenging to plan research around sprints for multiple initiatives. What if, while I empower others to run research, we use AI as a first round of user feedback? Felt so wrong to even consider this…since I’ve been trained to do the exact opposite — spend less time behind the laptop and expose the company to our users’ emotions and stories. After talking to a few other designers, and reading about companies as Synthetic users, I’ve started experimenting.

My goal was to create a UX feedback AI based skill that we can all use, to improve our work. The skill had to be aware of our business, be knowledgeable of our UX guidelines and be aware of users’ core goals and pain points. After trying a few overly complex set ups, among which was inevitably creating my own new shiny SaaS… I ended up with a skill in our repo. There were two things I’ve tweaked the most:

  • getting the skill to ask the right questions upfront to force people to reflect on the problem they’re solving.
  • providing the user perspective without extra interpretation.

The user perspective is already surprisingly good. It analyses the context of the prompt, then replies with how different users might react to the given solution, idea, etc. It does a good job of raising pain points and whether they are addressed across different kinds of interests people have. It’s not as good at providing specific usability feedback, besides the obvious stuff. AI reduces these user portraits to lines of text, ignoring all the other context they’ve built by using this and other software. This leads to some of the suggestions being overzealous, trying to explain every element through text and icons.

Product owners were the first to try out this part of the skill, to either help with setting a direction for tricky flows, or get more perspectives on a solution they’ve had in mind. In most cases, they brought the outcome of their session back to me and we continued the discussion. I was mostly surprised to see how often they also asked the skill to visualise its output, for them.

The skill also checks UI pattern usage against our guidelines and components. I underestimated this initially, but then noticed how front-end engineers got excited while demo-ing it. As our goal is to become much more consistent in the interface, the skill easily catches unnecessary deviations and provides recommendations pointing to relevant guidelines and elements. Front-end engineers could get immediate feedback on their work, instead of only manually checking guidelines. We didn’t try the full loop yet, as I’m tweaking the guidelines and the skill, but I think there’s something here that will lead to increased efficiency.

Ultimately, it’s not about replacing user research because it’s not as easy to get to people; we’re doing that anyway; it’s about catching critical misjudgments early on in the process.

Gathering context

There are quite a few people within the organisation playing around with different AIs, to become more efficient. One of these is centralising context, starting with documentation across our tooling, using Atlassian’s Rovo agents. These have been quite useful for me, as a newcomer to a very technical company, as I must prioritise impact on users’ experience.

Instead of digging through dozens of pages and boards, while throwing tons of basic questions at a team, I first ask different Rovo agents to collect context. A few prompts and some reading later, I have a basic understanding of a concept and when things get too technical, I ask them to simplify it using metaphors and analogies. In the end, this enables me to get in and out of topics much more efficiently, leaving more time to discuss what the real issues are to be solved, and what should be improved next. Lately, as these tools have been connected with other parts of the organisation, as support, we can tap into a great deal of evidence when collecting context and help steer the conversation better. I’d love to create some kind of mega shared context that eventually combines multiple data systems and our own skills or agents, working together. When someone wants to jump right into prompting solutions, or tends to have a single path to solving a problem, this shared context (tool?) would know which core issues to raise, with clear evidence, and push them to understand the problem first.

Conclusion

Useful overall, definitely not an extra designer, at least not yet.

It took me around 3 months to get comfortable with the shocking speed of AI, trying out new tools and new ways of working. When it comes to what’s being said nowadays about roles becoming more fluid within the design, engineering and product trio, I have mixed feelings. The best teams I’ve been in, had people who were always curious to understand how the others work, while trusting each other’s expertise. I must admit that using a shared tool does bring us a little closer. Can we really pour our expertise into these tools, so that others can genuinely step into our roles? Not sure yet. As a solo designer, AI hasn’t necessarily given me extra hands, but it has given me a lot of time back: time to test earlier, explore more alternatives, and frame problems better, together with the team.

Inspiration and further reading

I spent two months building an AI workflow for my design team. Here’s what I actually learned.

AI design isn’t ugly. It’s fluent — and that’s the problem.

Are synthetic users (really) the future of UX research?

Synthetic Users vs. Human Respondents: Same Conclusion, Less Variation

title: Machines are trying to get gut feelings while you’re telling me to ignore mine
text:
Machines are trying to get gut feelings while you’re telling me to ignore mine

Intuition was always treated as the second-best kind of knowing. Now AI is learning it from itself; we’re learning from AI, and nobody’s minding the loop. Welp.

I have a feeling about AI.

I know that’s an odd way to open an essay about AI, but hey, I’ve never been known as someone who presents as whatever the opposite of odd is. (Boring?)

Lately I’ve been really interested in the current discourse about taste and how it develops. Reading study after study, I kept noticing how hard all these people were working to quantify something I had always experienced as a kind of feeling.

I first ran into it at eleven, when I started wondering why I didn’t quite fit in with anyone. I tried very hard to work out what made everyone else a bit more usual than me, and I simply couldn’t name it. It was something inside me, not quite a feeling, but not just in my head either. It was why I found things beautiful that my friends found weird, why I loved the sound of certain music and definitely not whatever was trending, why I felt for the strange characters in books and, later, maybe even why I wasn’t attracted to the guys my girlfriends all chased after. It was certainly why I started writing poetry and dressing a little bit like Jesus on acid or, as my friend once called it, “techno amish”.

Weirdly, I started leaning into it more and more with age and have become much more confident about my being over the last couple of years. I also realized I somehow managed to build a career out of liking certain things and not others, and knowing how to communicate them. The oddness became part of my story and part of what makes me effective: at coming up with ideas, designing, writing, and especially at leading.

Yet, even now, decades into my so-called career, that thing I rely on most is still something I can’t really name.

It’s more than vibes but less than facts. I think.

Most people call it intuition. Some say the word affectionately, and some use it as a polite way of saying you can’t back something up or probably are a lil crazy.

I think it’s the most underrated skill we have, and right now, while every company I know is handing more of its judgment to a machine, it’s also the one we’re most likely to lose without noticing. I seem to be the only one worried about this, so this write-up is a way for me to make all of you aware and maybe, you know, sell you on my belief that it is absolutely essential to keep this planet spinning and us, happily, on it.

So what is it, actually?

I went looking for what science knows about intuition. It’s less mystical than I’d like (ugh), but kind of useful.

Most researchers describe it as pattern recognition built from experience, the kind that arrives before you can explain it. Daniel Kahneman called it System 1: fast, automatic, and usually right about things you’ve seen a thousand times.

I also checked the old cliché about women’s intuition, mostly because I was hoping for an easy fem-win. Women do score slightly higher on average at reading other people, but the gap is way smaller than I thought.

The biggest study so far tested more than 300,000 people in 57 countries and found a real but small difference. The psychologist William Ickes expected women to win his empathy tests easily. They didn’t. And when Kristi Klein and Sara Hodges paid people for getting it right, the gap vanished, because the men suddenly got better. So men can read a room perfectly well. They just tend to bother when there’s money on the table, which, if you’ve worked in tech, you may have suspected.

I’ll admit I was a little annoyed.

My whole thought-up argument about AI not being feminine enough to pick up vibes went out the window. What replaced it is kind of interesting, though: intuition isn’t a gift some people are born with. It’s a skill, built from years of noticing that someone is upset, or bluffing, or about to cry in a meeting, or that a plan looks right and isn’t. Skills can be learned, which means they can be taught. Possibly even to a machine.

Now this is something I’d like to sink my teeth into. Mostly because “Head of Vibes” is maybe the only title I’d get ridiculously competitive over.

My only chance at it, though, is if we admit it’s worth teaching. Historically, we haven’t.

The skill that was always second best at best.

The idea that men think and women feel goes back a long way.

Gerd Gigerenzer, a psychologist who has spent decades defending gut feelings, traces it from Aristotle all the way to the nineteenth century, and (spoiler!) it was never meant as a compliment.

Victorian scientists listed reliance on intuition next to emotional instability as one of women’s natural traits, which came in handy whenever someone needed a reason why women shouldn’t study, vote, or run anything.

In 1893, the sociologist Lester Ward gave “female intuition” its own chapter and decided it was an animal instinct for self-protection. I think he meant it kindly. It still reads like a nature documentary about a fairly clever badger.

So intuition became the consolation prize.

Men got reason, which counted.

Women got a feeling about things, which could be, you know, listened to, and then probably ignored. And because it was coded as female, the whole skill stayed undervalued, for everyone, long after women were let into the universities and the boardrooms.

But then why has intuition played such a big role in my life, career, and dare I say, success? My most viral talk (at Hatch this year) happened because I had a feeling I should talk about this. Most of my career growth happened because I had a feeling about things that turned out to be correct, and making them known early enabled my bosses to make better decisions and ultimately, ship cooler stuff.

While writing this, I listened to Jimmy Carr on Davina McCall’s podcast Begin Again, and he had a theory I can’t shake. All the woo-woo stuff, the crystals, tarot cards and horoscopes, is really just a talisman that lets women trust their intuition, because they can’t quite believe they know things. They need permission, and the cards give it to them. “They don’t believe in crystals,” he said. “They believe that they know something.”

I think he’s onto something that goes way beyond women and tarot. Most of us have been taught that what we sense doesn’t count until we can back it up, so we go looking for permission: a dashboard, data, a second opinion, a consultant’s deck, and now, more and more, a chatbot. Which is a funny thing to ask for permission from, since it’s the one thing in the room that has never had a gut feeling. It does have access to all of the world’s information, though, a great way to confirm a gut feeling. I haven’t made up my mind whether this is good or bad.

But intuition, no, AI doesn’t have it. Not yet, anyway.

Can it?

In 1966, the philosopher Michael Polanyi wrote that we can know more than we can tell. You can spot a friend’s face in a crowd of thousands, but you couldn’t write down how you did it. The economist David Autor later named this Polanyi’s paradox and used it to explain why automation kept eating the tasks we can describe step by step, while everything else stayed with people.

That held exactly until, well, recently.

In 2016, DeepMind’s AlphaGo played a move against Lee Sedol, one of the best Go players alive, that a human had about a 1 in 10,000 chance of playing. The commentators weren’t sure if it was brilliant or a bug. It won the game. Go had always been called a game of intuition rather than calculation, and the machine got there by playing itself over and over until it had something that looks a lot like a feel for the board.

Little caveat: a board game is exactly the kind of stable world Gigerenzer says machines are good at. Markets, customers, children and ourselves are not. For the messy, human kind of intuition, researchers are trying roughly two routes.

The first is to teach machines our judgment directly.

Most chatbots you use today were shaped by reinforcement learning from human feedback: instead of writing rules for a good answer, people compare two answers and pick the better one, thousands of times over. It’s built for tasks that are difficult to specify but easy to judge, which is pretty much the definition of intuition. We can’t explain what good looks like, so we keep pointing at it.

This is also how most modern evals basically work, and while I was excited to create and use them initially, it’s quickly become a rather monotonous task and one of my least-liked to-dos. I’d argue that’s because I need exactly 0 vibes to judge output. No vibes? Count me out.

The second route to getting intuition into machines is to give them something closer to lived experience.

Yann LeCun, one of the pioneers of modern AI, likes to point out that a house cat understands the world better than today’s chatbots, and he has started a company to build world models that learn the rules of the world from observation, like a baby learning about gravity. David Silver, who helped build AlphaGo, and Richard Sutton argue in their essay on the Era of Experience that AI is hitting the limits of what it can learn from human-written data, and that the next leap will come from agents learning from the world themselves.

So yes, I think machines will get some version of a gut. The real question is whose.

Two loops don’t mean infinity is close. Quite the opposite.

The uncomfortable part is that both routes can quietly turn into machines learning from machines.

Silver and Sutton’s agents are meant to be driven by their own experience rather than human judgment, and the human-feedback route leans more and more on feedback from other models. A 2024 study in Nature showed where that leads: models trained on content made by other models gradually forget what the real world looks like. The rare, odd cases disappear first, and after a few generations the output turns into nonsense. The researchers called it model collapse. I think it’s pretty obvious this is no solution to maintaining an equivalent to human gut feel. If it were, would we be drowning in slop? Clearly, machines love to just copy from each other.

Intuition lives in rare cases, the odd detail, the exception, the thing that doesn’t fit. A machine that learns its gut from other machines ends up with the average of an average.

No, thanks.

You can already feel it in the tools.

A thread on r/ClaudeCode with almost 400 upvotes complains that the newest Claude models got better at coding and worse at understanding people. The poster no longer trusts it to write anything users will read, because “it has no intuition for what a user wants.” One commenter asked for parts of a system to work like a kit and got a note about a naming conflict, because the model took the metaphor literally. LOL. Another, who says he’s a CS professor, guessed that models now learn more from AI feedback than from human feedback. Sure, that’s a hunch on Reddit, but it fits the pattern a little too well.

The second loop runs through us.

Intuition is trained on people, and if more of our day goes to talking with machines, we get fewer reps at reading actual humans: the pause after someone speaks, the tone of a message from the Chief of Staff, the client whose yes clearly means no.

A study by MIT and OpenAI found the heaviest ChatGPT users were also lonelier and socialized less, though nobody knows yet which came first. Researchers at Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon describe an old irony of automation: when the machine handles the routine stuff, people lose their daily practice of judgment and are rusty exactly when something unusual happens. And Sherry Turkle argues in her new book Artificial Intimacy that people start mistaking a chatbot’s agreeable empathy for the real thing, and then find real people too much work. Ugh. If I’m honest, I’m already seeing this in myself.

Put those together, and you get machines learning their instincts from each other while we learn ours from the machines. Everyone gets a little more average, and it all happens so obviously that nobody even calls a meeting about it. Scary.

I don’t want to live in that world. The mushrooms have shown me the point is to go further into my being, not away from it.

Who pays for it?

I’d love to say that people who trust their intuition, and women in particular, are harder to replace. But I’ve lived in the patriarchy long enough to know that’s bullshit, and the data doesn’t let me say it either.

The International Labour Organization found that jobs dominated by women are almost twice as exposed to generative AI as jobs dominated by men (29 percent against 16), mostly because so many women work in clerical and admin roles. Men still dominate the trades, and ChatGPT won’t be plastering your ceiling any time soon. Not that I’d stop it.

The bigger problem is that the work hardest to automate, reading people and spotting trouble early, doesn’t show up in job descriptions or get measured, so basically nobody gets paid for it. It happens in the gaps between the measurable tasks. When a company automates whatever appears in the spreadsheet and cuts headcount, that part disappears too, and nobody notices until things start falling apart or just feeling more shit (read: enshitification).

We spent centuries calling intuition irrational and leaving it to women, partly so it wouldn’t have to count.

Like, on purpose.

Now the machines are taking over the rational, rule-based work, and the part that’s left over, the hunch and the read on the room, is turning out to be the bit tech bros can’t teach their lil robots.

So, about that feeling…

Like any skill, intuition gets weaker when you stop using it. Every time a team overrules someone’s bad feeling because the dashboard looks fine, it gets a little better at ignoring the next one. And if machine intuition is going to be trained on human judgment, that’s a problem twice over, because a team that has stopped listening to its own gut has nothing left to teach with.

Keeping people with good instincts in the loop, and letting them actually use those instincts, might be one of the most important parts of building AI. I doubt it’s on anyone’s roadmap.

What can we do?

Leaders, treat “I have a bad feeling about this” as data, and ask what’s behind it. Everyone else, women especially, stop apologising when you say it. And if you’ve decided you’re just not an intuitive person, the research says you can do this too.

You just have to care about getting it right, which turns out to be most of what intuition is. I’d start by checking in with your body. And no, don’t worry, you don’t need to know the Zodiac to play or be into tarot.

I promised you a feeling about AI, so here it is.

It will get a gut eventually, and whether that gut is any good depends on whether there are still people around who trust theirs.

I plan to be one of them. Mine got me through a lot.

Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.

title: Future-proofing is dead and AI killed it
text:
Future-proofing is dead and AI killed it

We have always tried to build things that outlast whatever comes next. AI makes that impossible. The solution is the opposite of what you think.

When creating products, the goal is often to try and future-proof it.

Create a tool that won’t be obsolete in a few years. Learn the skill the machines can’t take.

Build the architecture flexible enough to survive whatever comes next.

Draw the roadmap that still makes sense down the line.

It’s been the sensible approach for decades, the thing you do so you’re not betting the company on something that could kill. That’s an understandable fear. S. Patrick Viguerie and his colleagues at Innosight actually found the average lifespan of a company on the S&P 500 has collapsed from sixty-one years in the late 1950s to under twenty, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.

The thing you bet on really does die faster than it used to.

But to be frank, that mentality just doesn’t work anymore. Future-proofing was always a bet that you could see far enough ahead to build toward it, and the speed at which AI is evolving how we create things, how we interact with things, how we collaborate with AI itself, has made that bet impossible to win.

France found this out the hard way almost a hundred years ago. After the First World War they built the Maginot Line, a wall of concrete and guns along the German border so strong no army could punch through it. It was the most future-proofed thing on the planet. Then the Germans drove around it, through the forest everyone swore tanks couldn’t cross, and took France in six weeks.

The wall worked exactly as designed, but the strategy of the warfare outsmarted it.

Future-proofing has the same flaw. You take your known experience and armor up against a war you can picture, but in reality, the war goes in a completely different direction.

In a slower era you at least got years between building the wall and watching someone flank it. In our age of AI those years are gone.

When ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, UBS analysts said they could not recall a faster ramp in twenty years of watching the internet, outpacing the nine months it took TikTok and the two and a half years for Instagram.

The situation gets worse, because we are no longer trying to predict just one thing that could change in the industry or technology or user habits. We are trying to predict three, all at once, all moving, all being shoved faster by the same technology.

The tech you build on.

The people you build for.

The company itself that you’re building.

Every one of them is a moving target, and future-proofing asks that we hit all three while they are in motion while we are standing on a platform that is moving too.

Let’s take them one at a time.

The tool you bet on is already dead

If we start with examining how companies rely on technology, it’s easy to see that people still pick the proven, well-funded, widely-used option because it seems like a safe bet.

Scott Brinker calls this Martec’s Law. Technology changes exponentially, and organizations change logarithmically. One curve shoots up, the other crawls, and the gap between what the tech can do and what your company can absorb gets wider every year.

Brinker was writing about marketing software, but the idea holds with where we are in the world of AI, and underneath that is Ray Kurzweil’s old observation that technology compounds on itself, each generation building on the last, so the pace does not just increase, the increase increases.

Patrick Neeman wrote a piece arguing the Double Diamond, the design process half the industry has leaned on for twenty years, is dead for software. His reasoning around this is what’s useful here, that the process was not wrong. The process was built for a world where making something was expensive and slow, so you spent a lot of time up front making sure you built the right thing before you committed. Then the cost of building a working prototype dropped from a two-week sprint to an afternoon.

One input fell by two orders of magnitude in under two years, and a process built on the way of working and pricing it survived into a world where that cost was no longer reasonable.

Future-proofing works exactly the same way. You pick the durable thing, the proven process, the safe stack, the tool with the big company behind it, because it feels like it will last, but that idea that it will continue to last is an illusion. Today, the thing that made it the right call at the time, the economics underneath it, is exactly what AI keeps disrupting.

Underneath all of this is a more straightforward problem. Future-proofing is a prediction, and people are famously terrible at prediction. Philip Tetlock spent decades studying expert forecasters, the people whose entire job is to see what is coming, and found they were barely better than chance, and sometimes worse than a crude rule of thumb.

These are the best-informed people in any room, and the future still makes fools of them regularly. Now hand that same impossible task to a product team and ask them to pick the tool that will still be right in three years, in the fastest technology shift any of us have worked through.

That’s just setting people up for failure where there are legit stakes.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

Let’s say you somehow beat the odds on the technology. You picked a stack or product that kept its place in the ranks of software. You still have the second problem.

AI is rewiring your user faster than you can build for them.

Think about what AI has done to the simplest thing a customer does, which is look for something. For twenty years, searching meant typing words into a box and scanning a page of blue links. People built entire companies, careers, and content strategies on that one stable behavior.

Natasha Sommerfeld and her team at Bain found that a large share of searches now end without anyone clicking through to a website at all, and that number climbs higher once AI starts answering the question directly instead of pointing at ten places that might.

The behavior that a generation of products was designed around is evaporating because of a technology most of those products never even considered.

It is not just search. Elizabeth Silliman and her colleagues at McKinsey surveyed around twenty-one thousand people about how they shop and found more than half already using AI somewhere in the process, with the behavior, in their words, shifting as fast as adoption itself, faster than the companies serving those customers can keep up.

The Capgemini Research Institute ran the same kind of study two years running, which is the useful part, because the year-over-year jump shows you the speed. This is not a new normal you can design for and settle into. It is a moving line.

Invoca, which sells software to marketers, found the share of people using a generative AI tool to research a serious purchase went from forty-one percent to fifty-eight percent in a single year. Among older buyers it tripled.

Imagine building a product around how your customer behaves, shipping it, and discovering that in the time it took to build, a third of them started researching an entirely different way. You tried to do everything right, but behavior just shifted to fast.

It doesn’t get better.

Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo, and Fasheng Xu studied what happens as people hand shopping over to AI agents, and found the scarce thing stops being the search and becomes the ability to say what you actually want, clearly enough for an agent to go get it. The whole shape of the interaction changes.

The thing you optimized, helping someone browse and compare, is not even the job anymore and, frighteningly, what you should have been designing for did not even exist when you started designing it in the first place.

This is the trap of the user you think you know. You do the research, you identify the behaviors, you ship the thing that fits who you think your audience is. By the time it hits the market, though, AI has given people a whole new set of habits and a new set of expectations that no longer fits.

Henry Ford supposedly said that if he had asked people what they wanted, they would have said a faster horse. The modern version is worse. Ask people what they want, and by the time you build it, the question itself has changed, because the thing answering their questions changed them while you tried to answer the original one.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you down

Keeping it going, let’s assume you somehow future-proofed the tech and kept up with the customer (well done!). There is still a third thing you cannot pin down, and it is your own company.

Every org is built around a set of assumptions about how work gets done.

Who owns what.

Who hands off to whom.

Which role exists to coordinate, which to decide, which to make the thing.

You draw that structure to be stable, because stability is the point of a structure. The moment AI changes how the work actually happens, that carefully drawn stability becomes the thing you have to fight.

Remember Scott Brinker’s philosophy that technology moves exponentially and organizations move logarithmically. The org is the slow curve by design, and the slowness you built on purpose, the clear roles, the defined ownership, the approval chain, is exactly what cannot bend when the fast curve jumps.

A design leader I know has been watching the traditional product owner role dissolve in his very large organization, because the work that justified it, coordinating the handoffs, chasing the status, translating requirements between teams, is precisely the work AI and a good design process now absorb.

The experience is the product, he told me, and the people who understand the experience can own it end to end. So where does that leave the role built to coordinate it? The hardest thing to change, he said, is not the work. It is that the taxonomy of roles is what funds the roles.

The org chart is not just how work flows. It is how budgets, titles, and headcount are justified. You cannot just delete a box on it, because someone’s job, someone’s comp, someone’s sense of what they are, is inside that box.

It’s not just him, research backs it up. Sam Ransbotham and his colleagues at MIT Sloan found that AI only delivers real gains when companies redesign the work around it, the roles, the workflows, the decision rights, and that where the structure stays frozen, AI just gets absorbed into the old process and changes nothing.

This is an old idea in organizational theory. Michael Hannan and John Freeman called it structural inertia, the tendency of roles, processes, and reporting lines to persist long after the conditions that created them are gone. The structure outlives its own reason for existing, and everyone keeps staffing it anyway.

Wolfgang Rohde, in a paper on AI and organizational capability, points out that companies discover the value of human judgment right after they have cut the roles that produced it. You optimize the org chart for the work AI can do, you thin out the people who caught the problems and trained the next ones, and then the first time something genuinely novel breaks, you find you removed the exact capacity you needed to handle it.

The future-proofed org is not just slow. It is brittle in a way you cannot see until it is tested.

Most companies are using AI to get better at things they already do, inside the structure they already have. David M. Rothschild and his colleagues at Microsoft Research call this choosing optimization over reinvention, because it is safer and easier to make the current machine a little faster than to admit the machine is the wrong shape.

The structure you built to protect the future becomes the single biggest reason you cannot meet it.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

All three of these problems end up having same answer. Stop trying to predict the future and lean into moving with it.

Trying to future-proof is no longer possible, so strategize and build to respond instead.

The most direct approach to this of this came from Jeff Bezos, years before the AI wave, in a letter to Amazon shareholders. He split decisions into two kinds. Some are one-way doors, irreversible, and those you make slowly and carefully, because you cannot walk back through them. Most decisions are two-way doors. You can walk through, see what is on the other side, and come back if you were wrong.

His warning was that as companies get bigger, they start treating every decision like a one-way door, applying the slow, heavy, careful process to choices that are easily undone, and they grind to a halt. Future-proofing is the one-way-door mindset applied to a world made almost entirely of two-way doors. You are deliberating like the choice is permanent when the whole advantage available to you is that it is not.

Nassim Taleb conceived a whole book around this posture. He called it being antifragile, designing things that gain from disorder instead of trying to predict and prevent it. A fragile thing needs the future to arrive exactly as forecast. An antifragile thing gets stronger when the future shows up weird, because it was built to absorb surprise rather than to bet against it.

Future-proofing is a bet that the future behaves. The reality is that now we have to build things, teams, and careers that do better precisely because it will not.

It is worth noticing that Brinker himself, the one who named the gap, never prescribed better prediction as the fix. His advice for living with Martec’s Law was to choose selectively which changes you take on, stay agile enough to move, and every so often reset your whole approach at an inflection point instead of defending the old one.

He never says get better at predicting. He spent his career proving companies can’t keep pace with the tech, and his answer is to stop trying to.

In practice this is less exotic than it sounds. David Hoang frames it as stop thinking of the work as a factory, a machine that turns a fixed input into a fixed output, and start thinking of it as a garden, something you cultivate and adjust as it grows and as conditions change.

A factory built for one product is worthless when the product changes. A garden just gets replanted.

When you do have to commit, Sundeep Misra points at the one thing worth being sure of, which is not the tool or the plan but the decision underneath it. The scarce skill in all of this is knowing what is actually worth building, so that when everything around it moves, you still know why you are moving.

Responding does not mean acting on every piece of feedback you receive. That sort of reaction can thrash the product to death and burn out your team. The important thing is to filter feedback based on the source and the perspective and real knowledge behind it.

Everyone has an opinion. The ones worth listening to are the informed ones, with genuine expertise and the right context. I tell founders this constantly. I will not weigh in on your code, because I am not the expert there, and my opinion should carry no weight with you on that topic, but when it comes to user experience or patterns around process, things I’ve seen a thousand times, then my opinion is valid.

This is just as true for you as it is for your company. You cannot future-proof yourself as an employee either, for the same reason. The specific skill you are banking on, the tool you mastered, the process you are known for, is exactly the thing AI commoditizes first.

The World Economic Forum estimates that 39 percent of workers’ core skills will be transformed or outdated between 2025 and 2030. Hoarding one skill and hoping it lasts is the personal version of the Maginot Line.

Stop armoring a fixed skill set and build the thing that does not expire, your judgment, your taste, your ability to learn the next thing fast and decide what is worth doing. That is the one capability AI is not coming for.

The answer to the anxiety that started all this is that you were right to be scared of betting the company on the thing that dies, but you were wrong about how to fix it.

We’ve seen that just building a better wall wasn’t the answer. France built the best one ever and still found themselves in a losing position.

Stop building to last.

Make reversible bets.

Stay close enough to your customers to feel the shift before it’s obvious.

Put your effort into deciding what’s worth building, not into guessing what survives. That’s what you can actually control.

References and further reading

The window has collapsed

  • S. Patrick Viguerie, Ned Calder and Brian Hindo, “2021 Corporate Longevity Forecast” (Innosight). The average lifespan of an S&P 500 company has fallen toward under twenty years, with roughly half the index expected to turn over within a decade.
  • Reuters, reporting the UBS analyst note, “ChatGPT sets record for fastest-growing user base” (2023). ChatGPT reached a hundred million users in two months, a pace UBS called unmatched in twenty years of wa
  • World History Encyclopedia, “Maginot Line.” The French fortifications that Germany bypassed through the Ardennes in 1940, now a byword for an expensive defense that offers a false sense of security.tching the internet.

The tool you bet on is already dead

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law: The Greatest Management Challenge of the 21st Century” (chiefmartec). Technology changes exponentially, organizations change logarithmically.
  • Ray Kurzweil, “The Law of Accelerating Returns” (2001). The exponential, compounding nature of technological change.
  • Patrick Neeman, “The UX Double Diamond Is Dead, and in AI Only One Survives for Software” (UX Collective). A durable process made obsolete when the cost of building collapsed.
  • Philip Tetlock, “Superforecasting” (2015) and “Expert Political Judgment” (2005). Expert prediction barely beats chance.

The customer you designed for just changed on you

  • Natasha Sommerfeld and colleagues, “Goodbye Clicks, Hello AI: Zero-Click Search Redefines Marketing” (Bain & Company, 2025). The zero-click shift and the reset of search expectations.
  • Elizabeth Silliman, Jack Trotter, and Kelsey Robinson, with Desirae Oppong and Shreya Jaggi, “Who Wins When AI Does the Shopping?” (McKinsey, 2026, around 21,000 consumers). AI shopping behavior shifting as fast as adoption.
  • Capgemini Research Institute, “What Matters to Today’s Consumer 2026” (12,000 consumers, year over year). The rate of change in AI-driven expectations.
  • Invoca, 2026 B2C Buyer Experience Report. GenAI purchase research rose from 41 to 58 percent in a single year.
  • Lingxiu Dong, Kaiwen Luo and Fasheng Xu, “From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce” (2026). As AI agents take over discovery, scarcity shifts from search to preference articulation.

The org chart you built is the thing slowing you do

  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). Organizations change logarithmically.
  • Sam Ransbotham, David Kiron, Shervin Khodabandeh, Sesh Iyer and Amartya Das, “The Emerging Agentic Enterprise: How Leaders Must Navigate a New Age of AI” (MIT Sloan Management Review with BCG, 2025). AI delivers gains only when roles, workflows, and decision rights are redesigned around it.
  • David M. Rothschild, Jake M. Hofman, Markus Mobius, Brendan Lucier, Eleanor Dillon, Daniel G. Goldstein, Nicole Immorlica, Aleksandrs Slivkins at Microsoft Research, “From Augmentation to Reconstruction: Guiding the AI Disruption to the Good Place” (2026). Most organizations use AI to accelerate pre-AI workflows; real change favors reconstruction over local optimization.
  • Wolfgang Rohde, “Short-Term Gain, Long-Term Fragility: AI Labor Substitution and the Erosion of Sustainable Capability” (2026). Organizations discover the value of human judgment after they have made it scarce.
  • Michael T. Hannan and John Freeman, “Structural Inertia and Organizational Change” (American Sociological Review, 1984). The foundational theory of why organizations resist changing their structure even after the conditions that shaped it are gone.

Stop armoring. Start moving.

  • Jeff Bezos, Amazon 2015 Letter to Shareholders. One-way-door versus two-way-door decisions, and the cost of treating reversible choices as permanent.
  • Nassim Nicholas Taleb, “Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder” (2012). Build to gain from disorder rather than predict it.
  • Scott Brinker, “Martec’s Law” (as above). His own prescription: choose selectively, stay agile, reset at inflection points.
  • David Hoang, “Software Gardens” (Proof of Concept, 2026). Cultivate the work like a garden, not a factory.
  • Sundeep Misra, “AI Won’t Save an Organization That Can’t Decide What to Build” (2026). The scarce skill is deciding what is worth building.
  • World Economic Forum, “The Future of Jobs Report 2025.” On average, workers can expect 39 percent of their existing skills to be transformed or become outdated between 2025 and 2030; judgment, adaptability, and continuous learning are the durable capabilities.
